title: The First Actual Bug
voice_direction: Calm, intimate museum-guide delivery at an unhurried pace; let 'Actual.' land slowly after a beat, a small smile on 'It was a joke', and a soft, settled final line.
narration: There is a moth in the Smithsonian, famous as the first computer bug. [pause] It wasn't the first bug. And the people who found it knew that. September ninth, nineteen forty-seven. Harvard University. The Mark Two, a calculating machine built for the U.S. Navy, ran on thousands of relays: little metal switches, clicking open and shut. At three forty-five that afternoon, the team found something in Panel F, Relay number seventy. A moth, caught between the contacts. They taped it into the logbook and wrote one line. "First actual case of bug being found." [pause] Read it again. Actual. Engineers had called glitches "bugs" for decades. In eighteen seventy-eight, Thomas Edison wrote of "bugs," "as such little faults and difficulties are called." So the note was never a discovery. [amused] It was a joke. Someone finally found a literal one. Grace Hopper, who worked on the Mark Two, told the story for years and made it famous. But the Smithsonian says the logbook probably wasn't hers, and no one knows for sure whose handwriting that is. In nineteen eighty-eight, it sat in a Navy museum, labeled with the wrong year. Today it's at the Smithsonian, moth still taped to the page. The most famous bug in history, [pause] and the punchline to a joke that was already old.

instagram_caption:
On 9 September 1947, at 15:45, the team testing Harvard's Mark II found something in Panel F, Relay #70: a moth, caught between the contacts.

They taped it into the logbook and wrote one line: "First actual case of bug being found."

The key word is "actual". Engineers had called glitches "bugs" for decades. In 1878 Thomas Edison wrote of "bugs", "as such little faults and difficulties are called". The note wasn't naming anything new. It was a joke: someone had finally found a literal one.

Grace Hopper, who worked on the Mark II, told the story for years and made it famous. The Smithsonian says the logbook was probably not hers, and no one knows for sure whose handwriting it is.

In 1988 the page sat in a Navy museum, labelled 1945. Today it is at the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History, with the moth still taped down.

facts.claim: On 9 September 1947 a moth was found in Relay #70, Panel F, of the Harvard Mark II (Aiken Relay Calculator) while it was being tested at Harvard
facts.source: Naval History and Heritage Command photo NH 96566-KN caption (NHHC Online Library, mirrored at ibiblio HyperWar); Computer History Museum, This Day in History, 9 September; Wikimedia Commons file description

facts.claim: Log entry reads '1545 Relay #70 Panel F (moth) in relay. First actual case of bug being found.'
facts.source: Jargon File 'bug' entry, citing Annals of the History of Computing vol. 3 no. 3 (July 1981) pp. 285-286; legible in NHHC photo NH 96566-KN

facts.claim: Engineers taped the insect into the logbook and labeled it 'first actual case of bug being found'; the logbook, with moth, is in the National Museum of American History (object 1994.0191.01)
facts.source: Smithsonian NMAH, 'Log Book With Computer Bug'

facts.claim: The logbook was probably not Grace Hopper's; she and the Mark II team helped popularise 'bug'/'debug'
facts.source: Smithsonian NMAH, 'Log Book With Computer Bug'

facts.claim: Hopper made the incident famous in her many public lectures
facts.source: Computer History Museum, This Day in History, 9 September

facts.claim: Who wrote the line is not settled (handwriting not Hopper's; sometimes attributed to operator William 'Bill' Burke, unconfirmed)
facts.source: Britannica, 'September 9: The First Literal Computer Bug'; Wikipedia 'Bug (engineering)'

facts.claim: Edison, 1878 letter to Theodore Puskas: 'Bugs' - as such little faults and difficulties are called
facts.source: Edison to Puskas, 13 Nov 1878, Edison Papers, cited in T. P. Hughes, American Genesis (1989) p. 75; IEEE Spectrum 'Did You Know? Edison Coined the Term Bug'

facts.claim: 'Bug' was engineering slang long before 1947, which is why the log says 'actual'
facts.source: JSTOR Daily, 'The Bug in the Computer Bug Story' (Matthew Wills); Jargon File 'bug'

facts.claim: Mark II: electromechanical relay machine built under Howard Aiken at Harvard, financed by the US Navy, completed 1947, later delivered to Dahlgren
facts.source: Wikipedia 'Harvard Mark II' (summary of Annals of the Computation Laboratory vol. 24, 1949)

facts.claim: In 1988 the log, moth still taped, was in the Naval Surface Warfare Center Computer Museum, Dahlgren, which dated it 9 September 1945 in error
facts.source: NHHC NH 96566-KN caption (photo courtesy NSWC Dahlgren, 1988); Wikimedia Commons file description
